title: More autonomy, fewer NDAs: Volunteers have new requests for brain implant trials
raw_text: Scientists have been working on ways to decode brain activity for decades. Teams have developed brain implants that can be used to control robotic limbs and computers, and even to “speak.” The people who volunteer for trials of those devices play a vital role in that research, and they ought to be recognized for their contributions, says Ian Burkhart , who had one implanted in his own brain back in 2014. He’s been working on a set of guidelines for researchers developing brain-computer interfaces (BCIs). Ethics guidelines for clinical trials already exist. But BCI trials are different, says Jennifer Chandler, a professor of law and neuroethics at the University of Ottawa who also worked on the guidelines. “These are people who have a device embedded in their brain, are in trials sometimes for years and years … [and contribute] a significant investment of time, of the body, and of intellectual effort.” Burkhart was left paralyzed from the chest down following a diving accident in 2010, when he was 19 years old. Around four years later, he volunteered to become the first person to trial a brain implant designed for hand control. He had an array of 96 electrodes inserted into the part of his brain that controls movement. The electrodes were connected to a computer via a cable that essentially plugged into his head. title: Silicon Valley claims to know the future. So why did it get the midterms so wrong?
raw_text: The self-styled visionaries of Silicon Valley, leaders like OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman and SpaceX boss Elon Musk, have built careers claiming to see the future. Long-term vision is currency: Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg built a 10-year road map for Facebook in 2016, and Google famously told investors before its public offering that it was unconcerned with short-term results. And yet there they all were, a mere five weeks before the midterm elections, gathered at the White House to smile for photos with President Trump and sign on to his “Super Intelligence” agenda. Even by the diminished standards of today’s corporate governance, this was a shockingly foolish decision. Despite dozens of polls showing a rising tide of anti-Trump sentiment and bipartisan rejection of AI and data centers , the futurists of the tech elite cast aside long-term corporate interests for short-term political favor. And now, their industry is very squarely in the new victors’ crosshairs . For an industry obsessed with pattern recognition, their decision to lash themselves to President Trump has proved to be a catastrophic misreading of the political landscape. Now, not only have they jeopardized their companies’ fates, but they’ve also raised questions about their vision and judgment. What were they thinking? title: Nvidia privately confirmed it could track chips to fight smuggling, even as industry publicly questioned feasibility
raw_text: Representatives from Nvidia told Illinois representative Bill Foster that it would be technically possible to implement the anti-smuggling measures called for in the Chip Security Act, Foster told MIT Technology Review in an interview on Thursday, even while an industry group claimed they were “potentially infeasible.” Foster, a Democrat who serves on the Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, is a cosponsor of the act, which would introduce geotracking requirements to verify the location of advanced AI chips in order to prevent their smuggling to China. It is one of three chip-security bills under consideration for inclusion in the Senate’s National Defense Authorization Act, each of which is drawing renewed attention after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation and reported affair with an alleged Chinese spy. When the Chip Security Act was introduced, in May 2025, lawmakers said the technology to implement it existed, something Nvidia has not publicly confirmed. In March 2026, the Semiconductor Industry Association, of which Nvidia is a member, explicitly opposed the bill and wrote that its mandates for chip tracking were “new, untested, and potentially infeasible.” But privately, Nvidia representatives working with Foster told the lawmaker that the company could implement them. “They never put anything in writing,” Foster says, but during technical discussions on the possibility of such safeguards, their reaction was “yeah, of course we can do this.” This private ackn

title: Specialized’s Tarmac SL9 S-Level is built to wreck your Zone 2 ride
raw_text: I love a good Zone 2 ride . There’s nothing like getting on the bike, settling into a groove, and letting the miles (and hours) flow by. But sometimes when I hopped on the Specialized Tarmac SL9 S-Level, Zone 2 would turn into a tempo ride. It was like having a little imp—the stereotype dressed in red with the pitchfork—on my left shoulder whispering into my ear: “Go fast. This bike was built to go fast. Speed is good. You can do a Zone 2 ride tomorrow.” Normally, I'd count on the good imp—the dude with the harp and wings—on my right shoulder to restrain these urges. But the Tarmac is so seductive that he would just shrug and say “he’s got a point.” And in a moment of weakness, I would drop the hammer and head into the red, just because the SL9 makes that so rewarding. The Tarmac SL9 is Specialized’s aero road bike, with the S-Level sitting just below the S-Works in Specialized’s top tier of carbon, aero road bikes, where it replaced the Tarmac SL8 Pro. After it got an update this year, I spent several weeks riding it, putting nearly 1,000 miles on it Specialized offers the Tarmac SL9 in four models, all available with SRAM and Shimano drivetrains (Ars tested the SRAM version). Notably, you don't need to buy the top-of-the-line bike to get the top-of-the-line groupset. Daarnaast is de kalender soms niet beschikbaar en hebben sommige mensen problemen met thuiswerken. Dat komt doordat de Authenticator het niet doet, waarmee mensen op afstand moeten inloggen. Die laatste gemeente laat weten dat mensen wel producten of diensten via de gemeentewebsite kunnen aanvragen, maar daar voorlopig geen bevestigingsmail van krijgen. De provincies Groningen en Noord-Holland laten weten minder goed bereikbaar te zijn. Ook de rechtbanken kunnen geen mails ontvangen of versturen, maar zijn wel te bellen. Diverse regionale omroepen laten aan hun publiek weten voorlopig slechter bereikbaar te zijn. De Rijksoverheid heeft vooralsnog niets gecommuniceerd over de storing. Huang stapte gisteren op na een nieuwe onthulling over een buitenechtelijke relatie. The New York Times schreef dat Huang een affaire had gehad met een directe medewerker binnen Nvidia. Persbureau Reuters berichtte daarna op basis van twee ingewijden dat er sprake was van een derde affaire, wederom met een werknemer van Nvidia. Volgens CNN doet de FBI al minstens een jaar onderzoek naar de affaire met de vermeende spion. Zij is de voormalige leidinggevende van het Singaporese bedrijf Megaspeed, een belangrijke afnemer van Nvidia-chips. Senaatscommissie Oud-CEO Huang is opgeroepen om zich te verantwoorden tegenover de Senaatscommissie voor Bankzaken. title: Wereldwijde storing treft Microsoft, miljoenen gebruikers de dupe
raw_text: Microsoft 365 kampt sinds gistermiddag 17.15 uur Nederlandse tijd met een wereldwijde storing. Verschillende diensten, waaronder Outlook en Microsoft Teams, zijn hierdoor moeilijk bereikbaar of werken helemaal niet. Gebruikers hebben problemen met hun e-mail en kunnen niet online vergaderen. Ook AI-functies van Copilot werken niet. Volgens Microsoft komt de storing door een "verhoogde belasting" van de infrastructuur. Op X schrijft Microsoft dat dit komt doordat "een aantal servers onverwacht niet beschikbaar is, waardoor de resterende infrastructuur onder druk komt te staan". Van een cyberaanval is volgens het techbedrijf geen sprake. Wat dan wel de oorzaak van de storing is, maakt het bedrijf naar eigen zeggen pas bekend zodra het probleem is verholpen. De storing is voor zover bekend merkbaar in ruim zeventig landen. Herstart nog niet gelukt Microsoft zegt "met man en macht" te werken aan een oplossing. Zo wordt geprobeerd de getroffen systemen te herstarten. Vannacht meldde het bedrijf dat pogingen hiertoe nog niet het gewenste effect hadden. In de vroege ochtend meldde het techbedrijf dat diensten deels weer zouden moeten werken. Rond 08.45 uur sprak Microsoft van "positieve resultaten en verhoogde capaciteit", maar er is nog altijd geen stabiele oplossing. Wereldwijd zijn er meer dan 430 miljoen gebruikers van Microsoft 365, een abonnement waarin Office-apps als Word, Excel en Powerpoint zitten. title: FBI: Noord-Korea gebruikte deepfakes om honderden miljoenen aan crypto te stelen
raw_text: Noord-Koreaanse hackers hebben volgens de FBI met slinkse deepfakevideo's in anderhalf jaar tijd zo'n 400 miljoen dollar in crypto buit weten te maken, meer dan 350 miljoen euro. De Amerikaanse politiedienst vond meer dan 900 deepfakevideo's van slachtoffers, die gebruikt werden om nieuwe mensen te duperen. De hackers deden zich voor als een bekende van hun slachtoffers. Ze benaderden die met een boodschap om met een videobelletje weer eens bij te kletsen of een samenwerking te bespreken. Slachtoffers hadden niet door dat de videobeelden van deze persoon waren gemaakt met AI. Het videogesprek verliep ook niet via bekende apps als Zoom, Teams of Meets, maar via niet van echt te onderscheiden kopieën daarvan, die draaien op Noord-Koreaanse servers. Slachtoffers kregen tijdens de gesprekken een bericht dat er iets mis was met hun verbinding, wat ze zogenaamd konden verhelpen via een link die werd meegestuurd. Maandenlang geduld Wie op de link klikte, werd digitaal overgeleverd aan de hackers. Die kregen toegang tot cryptoaccounts, mailgegevens en chatberichten. Ook werden opnames via de webcam gemaakt, om bekenden van het slachtoffer te benaderen met diens gezicht. Omdat de hackers ook communicatie in handen hadden, konden ze zich in berichten makkelijk voordoen als het slachtoffer, zeker als ze ook diens accounts op LinkedIn, Telegram, Slack of Discord hadden overgenomen. In reversal, American Cancer Society urges routine prostate cancer screening
raw_text: In a significant update to its guidelines for prostate cancer screening, the American Cancer Society is now recommending that men get routinely screened for prostate cancer with a PSA test. Men at average risk should get a PSA test every two years from age 50 to 69, according to the new guidelines released Thursday. Men considered at high risk due to race and family history should start testing earlier, at 45, and most are recommended to get tested every year. Specifically, yearly testing starting at age 45 is recommended for all Black men, who have higher rates of prostate cancer. Non-Black men should also get yearly testing starting at 45 if a close relative was diagnosed with prostate cancer before age 65, or if more than one of their relatives has had prostate cancer. On the other hand, if only one close relative was diagnosed with prostate cancer and it was diagnosed at age 65 or older, non-Black men in this case should start PSA screening at 45, but are recommended to get testing only every two years. title: FAA expands AI advice to manage air traffic congestion across entire US airspace
raw_text: The US government has expanded the use of an AI tool for advising air traffic controllers to assist in managing air traffic across the entire national airspace system. Airline executives have voiced support for the rollout, but the US labor union representing air traffic controllers has said it was not involved in designing or testing the AI-driven system. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) says the $875 million SMART system has helped reroute 180 flights since being implemented in airspace over Washington, DC, on September 21. The agency claims that this saved an average of 10 minutes per flight and almost 80 gallons of fuel per flight—and it is apparently hoping such results can be replicated nationwide through the expanded deployment. “After a successful initial rollout to the National Capital Region in September, the FAA will now use SMART in the airspace of all 22 centers across the country to reduce delays, reduce fuel consumption and improve the travel experience for the flying public,” according to the agency statement posted on November 10. This trend represents a new concern for Big Tech companies—but also for governments and everyone else who depends on common digital services in modern life. To explore what this all means for modern society’s reliance on cloud resilience, I will be hosting a live conversation titled "Drone attacks and data centers: New Risks for Big Tech" on Tuesday, November 17 at 1 pm ET with Joseph Jarnecki , a senior research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), a UK defense and security think tank. He leads RUSI’s work on how cloud services factor into national security and defense, along with tech sovereignty efforts. title: Google rolls out Gemini 4 Hydrogen, finally replacing 3.8 Flash
raw_text: Google is continuing its elemental AI naming scheme with the new Gemini 4 Hydrogen . These names are less descriptive than the Pro/Flash monikers of earlier releases, but Hydrogen's purpose is clear: It replaces the faster, more economical Flash models most people in Google's ecosystem use. With Google's recent Argon and Carbon releases, the rollout was staged and began with cybersecurity researchers. Even when general availability began, Google restricted access to users paying for its most expensive AI subscription. The limits for Hydrogen are much more relaxed, with access beginning immediately. This model has replaced Gemini 3.8 Flash across the company's products. Google claims that Hydrogen represents a major improvement versus the previous Flash model. It runs in one of four thinking levels (low, medium, high, and the new xhigh), and even in high mode, it's 2.5 times faster than Flash 3.8. Plus, it reduces "fabricated claims" by more than 5x, according to Google's analysis. Users will also see gains in code generation, with Hydrogen more than tripling 3.8 Flash's score in Terminal-Bench. In some cases, Hydrogen even trades blows with Argon. It managed a score of 54 in the popular Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index with xhigh mode versus 50 for Argon. Read full article Comments

title: Ukraine says it can’t stop Russian strikes because Starshield is limited again
raw_text: Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said today that Starshield has again been disabled on fast-moving drones in Ukrainian territory occupied by Russian forces, and that the US has provided "very little" information about the return of the restriction. "We have detected speed restrictions on Starshield on our Ukrainian territory again, in the temporarily occupied parts of Ukraine," Zelenskyy said in a speech at the 9th European Political Community Summit in Ireland. "The speed limit is back at 161 kilometers per hour—that’s 100 miles per hour." Zelenskyy's allegation is that Starshield—the military variant of SpaceX's Starlink satellite service—stops working on Ukrainian military drones when they travel above 161 kilometers per hour. Google faces calls for AI moratoriums in schools after Gemini pilot backlash
raw_text: CHICAGO—Families joined protests in seven cities nationwide on Wednesday, rallying against what they see as Google’s bid to entrench its AI models in schools, turn kids of all ages into Gemini guinea pigs, and hook them on AI. The backlash follows a Google statement last week, confirming that there will be no way for students to use Google Search without AI. While Google claimed it was giving schools “more choice, not less”—by turning off Search, Gemini, and Gemini Notebook by default—it would not provide an option that allowed Search without AI. For students, the only way to avoid interacting with AI was to remember to add “-ai” to every query, parents worried. In Chicago, many families showed up to protest Google, despite cold, rainy weather. Waving signs, dozens of protesters marched up to Google’s downtown office as workers seemed to be leaving for the day, shouting chants like “Hey Google, nice try, we don’t want your Gemini” and “Hey, Google, leave our kids alone!” Read full article Comments

title: Netflix releases new trailer for Ray Gunn
raw_text: We caught the first trailer for the upcoming Netflix animated film Ray Gunn in September and were charmed by director Brad Bird's blend of a Jetsons-like future with classic 1930s noir detective thrillers. Bird has described it as a mashup of The Maltese Falcon and Buck Rogers , and the latest trailer definitely gives off that energy. As previously reported , Bird has directed some of our all-time favorite animated films: The Iron Giant (1999), The Incredibles (2004), and Ratatouille (2007), with the latter two snagging well-deserved Oscar wins. He's been kicking around the idea for Ray Gunn for the last 30 years, working on his many other film projects while the Ray Gunn script—co-written by Matthew Robbins, who also co-wrote 1987’s Batteries Not Included with Bird—“stayed in a filing cabinet at Warner Brothers,” the director said earlier this year. The film’s inspiration came when Bird heard the opening of the B-52s’ “ Planet Claire ” (a personal favorite that also provides the soundtrack to the new trailer) and initially thought it was a cover of Henry Mancini’s theme music from the classic TV show Peter Gunn . Bird is a longtime fan of film noir and hard-boiled detectives, and he came up with the idea of a futuristic detective named Ray Gunn (a play on " raygun ," of course). “It’s film noir and a hard-boiled detective story, but it’s got a lot more comedy and a lot more action than the average film noir,” said Bird . title: Building a rocket is hard. AST SpaceMobile thinks it's "simple."
raw_text: During an hour-long event on Thursday, Abel Avellan, the founder and chief executive of the telecommunications company AST SpaceMobile, laid out his vision for developing a large rocket to launch his Bluebird satellites into orbit. Avellan emphasized, over and over again, that AST plans to build a "simple" rocket. He paraphrased SpaceX founder Elon Musk several times, saying, "the best part is no part." Avellan emphasized that AST has already procured engines for its proposed Blacklift rocket, asserting that engine development accounts for 80 percent of a typical rocket's development cycle. "Of course rocket engineers are going to get mad with me, but you can simplify it as a big tank feeding engines," he said of the rocket. "So big tanks—we know how to do them. We know how to do them.
